problem: Geometry-based mapping-and-planning navigation abstracts away physical and semantic traversability (tall grass looks blocked, mud looks passable), while learning from simulators or human labels/demonstrations is limited by simulator fidelity or does not improve with more data.
motivation: Real-world navigation violates geometric assumptions and exhibits exploitable patterns. Learning directly from real robot experience grounds traversability in actual outcomes and improves as more data is collected, giving a network effect as more robots are deployed.
key_idea: Train low-level goal-conditioned navigation skills and their distance functions from real experience, then use those skills and distances as learned abstractions to build topological 'mental maps' for high-level planning and exploration.
insight: The paper's core message is that low-level learned capabilities should define the abstractions (graph connectivity via D(o_t,o_g)) used by high-level planning, so different robots get different maps. Goal-conditioned imitation, RL, and offline RL share the same structure (relabeling goals plus an action-favoring objective). Side information such as GPS and overhead maps is best used as a heuristic in the high-level planner, not as input to the low-level skill. There are no ablations, since this is a tutorial/review of prior work.
method: Experiential learning principle: learn from real trajectories (offline, online or both) rather than human labels, simulators or blind imitation; the task is defined by a goal observation.
Goal-conditioned low-level policy π(a|o_t,o_g): trained with supervised hindsight relabeling g(τ,t) (log-likelihood), Q-value objectives (DDPG/SAC/CQL) or weighted likelihood (AWR/AWAC/CRR).

Distance function D(o_t,o_g): the negative value function from RL with reward -1 per step, or a regression onto time-step differences in the dataset (t'-t); it predicts how long the skill takes and whether it succeeds.

Topological mental map: a subset of stored observations forms graph nodes with edges weighted by D. Graph search yields the next waypoint, which the low-level policy executes (ViNG, no explicit localization).

RECON exploration: a variational information bottleneck gives a latent subgoal z_g from the conditional encoder q(z_g|o_g,o_t) with prior p_0. Fringe exploration goes to low-visitation graph nodes and samples random latent subgoals.

ViKiNG heuristics: a contrastive-learned heuristic model takes an overhead map/satellite image, a noisy GPS goal and a query location, and predicts reachability. It serves as an A*-style heuristic that also accounts for the robot's travel time.
BADGR/LaND low-level skills: model-predictive skills from random-collected data predict collision, bumpiness and position, and LaND adds human disengagement prediction to learn sidewalk semantics.

setting.backbone: Various deep networks from prior works (BADGR, LaND, ViNG, RECON, ViKiNG); no new model here
setting.training_data: Real-world robot experience; ViNG/RECON low-level models use about 40 hours of data across many environments, with tens of minutes per environment for the map; BADGR uses randomly collected data; LaND uses human disengagements
setting.observation: monocular forward-facing RGB camera (no depth/GPS/LiDAR for the low-level skills); overhead satellite maps and noisy GPS for ViKiNG's heuristic
setting.privileged: none at the skill level; ViNG needs a prior traversal of the environment to build the map, and ViKiNG uses GPS/overhead maps as side information

numbers_note: Tutorial/review article; no quantitative tables reported. Results are only qualitative and shown in figures.
results: The article reports qualitative outcomes from earlier papers only. LaND navigates real Berkeley sidewalks, ViNG performs autonomous mail delivery, RECON explores novel environments to reach image goals, and ViKiNG reaches goals up to 2 km away in unseen environments (a 1.2 km run with no interventions). No benchmark comparisons are given.
limitations: Learned representations are hard to interpret and debug, and no validation-set equivalent exists for learning-based control.
Safety and robustness are unresolved, and robust uncertainty estimation and out-of-distribution handling are needed.
Dataset coverage and curation are critical, and the reviewed methods are mostly short-horizon and need prior exploration or side information.
